earliest_print_source: First Things First, Stephen R. Covey with A. Roger Merrill and Rebecca R. Merrill, 1994
notes: The clock/compass framing is the organizing metaphor of the opening of First Things First (1994): the clock stands for commitments, schedules and how we spend time; the compass for vision, values and what matters most; and Covey names the gap between them. This wording is a condensed rendering of that passage rather than a verbatim sentence I can pin to a page, so I withhold the top of the scale. The author name in the record is misspelled: it is Stephen R. Covey, not Steven Covey.

The voice is strongly consistent with Stuart Wilde (1946-2013) — the irreverent register, the ego-as-taskmaster conceit, the closing 'I wouldn't stand for that BS if I were you' — and the line circulates consistently under his name. It plausibly comes from Infinite Self (1996) or Silent Power, but I cannot place it in a specific book or page from training knowledge, so I will not name one.

Circulates widely as an unsourced 'Sufi saying' or 'Sufi epigram' in English-language quotation collections. I know of no Sufi primary text, named poet, or translator behind it, and the polished English antithesis (heart grieves / spirit rejoices) reads like a modern anthology formulation. Generic tradition labels of this kind are effectively unverifiable.

I have no knowledge of Sukh Chugh as a published author, and no recollection of this passage in any book, essay, or collection. The prose reads like contemporary personal-blog or social-media writing. Attribution may well be correct, but I have nothing to confirm it against.

Swami Amar Jyoti (1928-2001), founder of Truth Consciousness, published satsang discourses (Spirit of Himalaya, Retreat Into Eternity) and the line is idiomatically plausible for that body of work. I cannot place it in any specific discourse or volume, and it does not appear in quotation references I can recall.

Genuinely Vivekananda in substance and idiom; 'We are what our thoughts have made us' is a recurring formulation of his and the passage is consistently cited to the Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda. I cannot confirm the volume, lecture, or page from training knowledge, so I leave the print source blank rather than guess a locator. Held below the promotion bar for that reason.

Usually labeled a Swedish proverb in English collections, sometimes simply 'proverb'. I know of no traceable earliest appearance, no Swedish original I can cite, and no scholarly proverb reference that dates it. An honest 'unknown'.

earliest_print_source: Self-Help, Samuel Smiles, 1859 (quoting the Rev. Richard Cecil)
notes: 'Sydney Smiles' is not a person; this is a corruption of Samuel Smiles, the Scottish author of Self-Help (1859). In Self-Help, Smiles quotes the maxim from the Rev. Richard Cecil, whose usual wording is 'The shortest way to do many things is to do only one thing at once' — so even under the corrected name Smiles is the transmitter, not the author. My recollection of the Self-Help citation is good but not page-level; the confidence figure reflects the weakness of the attribution as recorded, not of the reattribution.
suggested_reattribution: Richard Cecil, as quoted by Samuel Smiles in Self-Help (1859)

notes: A well-documented misattribution. Eliot never wrote this; it appears in Marthe Troly-Curtin's novel Phrynette Married (1912) as 'Time you enjoy wasting is not wasted time', and Quote Investigator traced it there. Wikiquote lists it in the misattributed section of the Eliot page. Low confidence here reflects the near-certainty that the recorded attribution to Eliot is wrong.

earliest_print_source: Preface to Transit of Venus: Poems by Harry Crosby, T. S. Eliot, 1931
notes: Genuine Eliot. The line comes from his preface to Harry Crosby's posthumous collection Transit of Venus (Black Sun Press, 1931), and Wikiquote carries it as sourced. I am confident in the work and year but have not verified the exact wording against the preface, so I stop short of 'verified'.

earliest_print_source: Dante, T. S. Eliot, 1929 (reprinted in Selected Essays, 1932)
notes: Genuine and well-sourced Eliot, from his 1929 monograph Dante, which was collected in Selected Essays. The sentence is quoted verbatim in the standard references and the wording in the record matches.

earliest_print_source: The Sacred Wood: Essays on Poetry and Criticism, T. S. Eliot, 1920 ('Philip Massinger')
notes: Genuine Eliot, from the essay 'Philip Massinger' in The Sacred Wood (1920). The record quotes only the opening clause; the full sentence continues '...bad poets deface what they take, and good poets make it into something better, or at least something different.' Truncation is standard in quotation but worth noting, since the fuller line reverses the cynical reading the short version invites.

earliest_print_source: Seven Pillars of Wisdom, T. E. Lawrence, 1926 (introductory chapter)
notes: The author field is wrong by one initial: this is T. E. Lawrence (Lawrence of Arabia), not T. S. Lawrence — almost certainly contaminated by the neighbouring T. S. Eliot entries. The passage is from the introductory chapter of Seven Pillars of Wisdom (1926) and the wording in the record matches the standard text.

Consistently attributed to Tarthang Tulku in quotation collections and idiomatically consistent with his Dharma Publishing books (Skillful Means, Gesture of Balance, Knowledge of Freedom). I cannot locate it in a specific book or chapter, so no print source is offered.

Same situation as the preceding Tarthang Tulku line: plausible in voice and consistently attributed to him in secondary collections, but I can place it in no specific work. Slightly weaker than q_1319 because it circulates less and the phrasing is more generic.

Authentically Teilhardian in both doctrine and phrasing — love as the physical energy that draws fragments toward convergence is central to his cosmology — and the line is consistently attributed to him. However, sources differ on the work (variously The Phenomenon of Man, Human Energy, and the essays collected in Toward the Future), and I cannot resolve which is correct or confirm the translation, so I name no source. Full name is Pierre Teilhard de Chardin.

Terri Guillemets is a contemporary American quotation anthologist (The Quote Garden) who also writes original aphorisms, and this is one of hers rather than an anonymous line she collected. Attribution is consistent wherever it appears. Original publication is self-published online rather than in print, so there is no print source to cite and no independent scholarly confirmation.

earliest_print_source: Apologeticus (The Apology), Tertullian, c. 197 AD, ch. 9
notes: Genuine Tertullian, rendering 'etiam fructus omnis iam in semine est' from Apologeticus ch. 9. Important context: it is not a general aphorism about potential — Tertullian is arguing against abortion ('he is a man who is going to be one; the whole fruit is already present in the seed'). Anyone using the line as a standalone metaphor should know the argument it belongs to. Confidence held at 0.8 because I am recalling the chapter from memory of the Latin, not verifying an edition.

earliest_print_source: The Book of Job 12:8, King James Version, 1611
notes: Accurate KJV text. The full verse reads 'Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee.' Citation in the record (Job 12:8) is correct; the quoted fragment is the first clause.

The sentence is idiomatically ACIM — wholeness, lack, and demand are its standard vocabulary — and it is consistently attributed to the Course. But ACIM is a large text with a precise numbering system (T-/W-/M- locators), and I cannot place this line at any chapter or section. Without a locator I will not assert the source. Also note the title is A Course in Miracles, not 'The Course in Miracles'.

This is an item from the chain-circulated list 'Instructions for Life in the New Millennium', which spread by email in the late 1990s under the Dalai Lama's name. The Office of the Dalai Lama has disclaimed the list; it is not his, and several of its items track secular American self-help writing (H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s Life's Little Instruction Book is often noted as a source of similar material). Wikiquote treats the list as misattributed. I cannot identify the actual author of this specific line, so I offer no reattribution. A classic misattribution magnet — treat any bare 'Dalai Lama' aphorism in this register with suspicion.

earliest_print_source: Gospel of Thomas, saying 70 (Nag Hammadi Codex II, c. 2nd century CE); English in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 1977
notes: Saying 70 of the Coptic Gospel of Thomas, recovered at Nag Hammadi in 1945. The Coptic is damaged and translations vary considerably — several render it 'That which you have will save you if you bring it forth from yourselves; that which you do not have within you will kill you if you do not have it within you.' The elegant parallel wording in the record is one translation tradition (popularized via Elaine Pagels and Joseph Campbell), not the only one. The attribution to the text is solid; the exact English is translator-dependent.

earliest_print_source: Isha Upanishad 6-7; this English rendering from The Ten Principal Upanishads, trans. Shree Purohit Swami and W. B. Yeats, 1937
notes: The source text is certain: Isha Upanishad verses 6-7, on seeing all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings, therefore knowing no hatred or sorrow. The distinctive English phrasing ('Of a certainty...') I believe is the Purohit Swami/Yeats translation rather than Mascaro or Radhakrishnan; I am confident enough to name it but flag it as a translation identification, not a verified collation. The author field would be more precise as 'Isha Upanishad' than the general 'Upanishads'.

I know of no Vedic passage corresponding to this, in any standard translation. The epigram's shape — a chiasmus about using memory rather than being used by it — is a modern rhetorical form, and 'The Vedas' is exactly the kind of blanket ancient-authority label that gets attached to unsourced aphorisms. Very likely modern and pseudo-attributed, but since I cannot name a real author I am not calling it a misattribution outright.

Consistently attributed to the poet Theodore Roethke (1908-1963) across quotation collections, with no competing claimant that I know of. It most likely comes from his notebooks rather than the published poems — Straw for the Fire: From the Notebooks of Theodore Roethke (ed. David Wagoner, 1972) is the usual candidate — but I cannot confirm that, so I name no source. Consistent attribution without a locatable text keeps this below the promotion bar.
